frase_gancho.texto: A basket woven in a spiral over months, from the fibers of the desert.

puente_narrativo.texto: From weaving we move on to wood. Look for the figure of an animal, carved from a dark wood, polished until it shines, so heavy that it sinks in water.

guion_corto.texto: This large spiral-woven plate is a corita, made by the women of the Comcaac (Seri) people, who live on the coast of the Sonora desert, facing the Gulf of California. It is woven from the fibers of the torote, a desert shrub: a bundle of fiber is coiled, and then stitched round after round with the help of a bone awl. Roots and bark are used to dye part of the fiber, and that is how the reddish-brown geometric designs appear. It is extremely slow work: a large basket can take months or even years. It ends up so tightly woven that, it is said, it can hold liquids. More than a container, it is a source of pride for the weavers and a symbol of abundance.

guion_largo.texto:
Comcaac means “the people.” The Seri, as others call them, are a small people, of around a thousand individuals, who live in Punta Chueca and El Desemboque. For centuries they roamed the coast and Tiburón Island, the largest island in Mexico, and lived from fishing, hunting, and gathering. Their language is unique: no sure relatives are known for it, making it what linguists call a language isolate. In other words, a language that has been walking alone for a very long time.

Unlike the Yaqui and the Rarámuri, whose languages are cousins of Nahuatl, Seri is the exception. And it is also an exception in its way of life: people of the sea and of the desert at the same time, who learned to draw from the dry coast everything they needed.

Watch how the corita is born. Everything begins at the center, with a small knot, and from there the basket grows in a spiral, round after round, each one stitched to the one before. It is a single spiral that never breaks. In the [desert petroglyph](mna_s11_petroglifo_desierto) you saw below, hunters engraved spirals a very long time ago. We do not know whether there is a connection, but the desert seems to repeat that shape again and again.

The work begins far from the workshop. It is said that the weavers walk long distances to choose the longest, straightest torote branches, then dry them and split them into very thin strips. Afterward, with infinite patience, they stitch them with the deer-bone awl. Each stitch is pulled tight so that no space is left between one round and the next. That is why the basket turns out so firm and, it is said, can even hold water.

Coritas were everyday containers, used to store seeds or gather food. Today they are also appreciated as art, and many are made for collectors and museums. That has changed the tradition, but it has also given the weavers recognition and an income. For many families, weaving is a women’s craft, passed down from grandmothers to granddaughters.

The designs, according to specialists, may evoke the surroundings: the wind, the dunes, the spines of the cactus, the tracks of the loggerhead turtle. Each weaver combines them in her own way, so no two coritas are identical. Notice how the reddish-brown color contrasts with the golden tone of the fiber: it is like looking at the desert at sunset.

The loggerhead turtle, which appears in designs and sculptures, holds a very important place in the life of the Seri. You will see it again in the next piece, turned into wood. The corita and the sculpture are two ways of saying the same thing: that the Comcaac people live in dialogue with their land.

As with the looms you saw in the previous halls, here too knowledge passes from hand to hand, by watching and repeating, without school or books. Whoever weaves a corita keeps in it time and knowledge: which plant to use, where it grows, how it is dyed. She does not simply make an object; she sustains a way of reading the desert, and of continuing to live in it.

texto: Follow with your eyes the spiral that begins at the center
Look for the reddish-brown designs on the golden fiber
Notice how tight the stitches are

texto.Region: Sonoran Desert Coast (Punta Chueca and El Desemboque / Tiburón Island)
texto.Technique/Material: Soft limberbush fiber (Jatropha cuneata), plant dye from dark limberbush, and burnishing
texto.Function: Sacred basketry, seed container, marine gathering, and traditional sumptuary art

texto.pregunta: Myth: Baskets are just simple containers.
texto.respuesta: Reality: A large corita can take months or years of work, and it is one of the most prized basketry traditions in Mexico.
